description:
Greetings from Team Sferavis!

You may call us a group of astrophiles and certainly astronomy brought together across borders by our shared love to chase the infinity. With plenty amount of curiosity, a little chaos, and, inevitably, a few mistakes, we’re taking on the challenge of creating another eye for the humanity. Between the science, the experiments, the bugs, and the laughs, we're ready to see how much of the unseen universe we can bring into view with NASA's SphereX.
summary: Sferavis serves as a free, public web tool based on NASA's SPHEREx catalogs, allowing users to live in the infrared sky. It uses a celestial sphere with both simulated and real data from different datasets and gives users full freedom in celestial navigation. It offers different tools, including light curves and spectroscopy, and, on top of that, allows users to compare the sky across all available epochs to detect unlabeled moving objects in the celestial sphere. The detection runs on a Python pipeline that downloads SPHEREx data, performs PSF subtraction, preprocesses the data, detects and labels objects by cross-checking them against available catalogs. After completing the processing, it identifies tracklets of moving objects across different epochs, extracts their spectra, and finally classifies the objects based on a classification index developed by our team. The documentation, publications, and tutorials, along with the Redium AI bot, help users have the best experience exploring the unseen sky and seeing the pixels that cannot be seen with our eyes.
details:
Vision

Sferavis is a platform where we try to interact with users beyond the limits of our eyes. Throughout the project, we have tried to create an environment that allows people to see the sky in infrared and understand what the sky looks like in the infrared region. Sferavis is basically a project developed by a team of astrophiles who literally live under these night skies. Still, the sky felt so unfamiliar when we saw it in the infrared band. Using NASA's SPHEREx mission, we can build a sky across a much broader range of wavelengths.

Sferavis Atlas: The Real-time Sky Simulator

In the Sferavis Atlas, we have built both a simulated environment that allows users to work with and navigate through SPHEREx catalogs, and an option to view the actual FITS files from SPHEREx data to create a planetarium-like interface for users, with proper representations of Zodiacal Light, Diffuse Galactic Light, and dust maps. Here, users can simulate their sky for any time and place, and it clearly matches the sky in the Sferavis Atlas, giving them a real-time experience. Along with that, we are incorporating magnitudes on the infrared scale, allowing people to compare the sky in visible and infrared bands in real time.

Moving Objects, Epochs, and Multi-Survey Inspection

We are retrieving asteroids and comets using NASA-JPL datasets, which can encourage people to detect moving objects effectively. When a user selects a region of the sky, we immediately query SIMBAD and WISE data to provide views from other surveys, as well as identify the selected patch of the sky. Clicking on the 'Inspect SPHEREx Epochs Here' option allows users to compare SPHEREx tiles from different epochs. We also encourage users to change the FoV to detect both fast-moving and slow-moving objects. From the different MJD epochs and different wavelengths, we are creating a lightcurve and spectrum for any object along with a Catalogue SED view which takes 2MASS, AllWISE and Gaia magnitudes from VizieR.
Users can flag a tile if they believe they have found a moving object which then can be matched with our pipeline and we can confirm the object.

Data Pipeline and Classification

On the other hand, the pipeline selects a portion of the sky requested by the users, detects sources using SExtractor, matches the objects with Gaia, SIMBAD, and 2MASS data, and performs PSF subtraction. It then creates CSV files containing moving and static objects, both labeled and unlabeled. After extracting their spectra, it can classify objects as planets, supernovae, quasars, stars, galaxies, asteroids, or comets.

Learning Support

Sferavis has the potential to be a guide for learners who are unfamiliar with the infrared sky. It has an AI assistant that can help users whenever they get stuck on the website. We also inspire users to flag new objects to provide more candidates for cross-checking through our pipeline. Along with that, we have prepared handwritten tutorials and videos generated using Google NotebookLM to give users a clear understanding of astronomical objects and the features they should look for to classify an object accurately. We expect to generate a large number of candidates to detect our new asteroid or stellar friends in the path of infinity.

Tech Stack and Data Resources

We tried to develop our pipelines entirely in Python, while JavaScript was used to project and visualize the infrared sky. In terms of visualization technologies, we used WebGL2 and Canvas 2D. Regarding data services and astronomical resources, we used CDS HiPS2FITS and HiPS, SIMBAD, VizieR, IRSA, the JPL Small-Body Database, WiseView, Legacy Surveys cutouts, Wikipedia, IRSA TAP, Gaia DR3 (through the ESA Archive and VizieR mirrors), SkyBoT, and Miriade. For building the website TypeScript, JavaScript, CSS and HTML were used in assistance with Google Ai Studio, GitHub Copilot, ChatGpt Codex and Claude Code.

Cross-Survey Experience and Planetarium Interface

The creativity in this project comes to see the sky in different surveys. In the same celestial sphere, we are seeing an object with SPHEREx, WISE, Optical surveys which essentially develops our idea of how each astronomical object behaves in each of the wavelengths or in different surveys. Sferavis turns a survey archive into a place you can stand in. Most SPHEREx tools show tables, cutouts or plots. We built a planetarium where you choose your latitude, longitude and time, look up at the infrared sky, and tap any spot. From that one tap you get the object’s name and a plain-language description, its WISE images from 2010 onward, and a blink comparator across SPHEREx epochs. You can also read a low-resolution spectrum from the same spot. The interface gives anyone a way to see change, which is what SPHEREx’s repeated observations are for and the tutorial builds the intuition of the spectrum of a particular astronomical object and its behaviour.

Accessibility, Speed, and Scientific Grounding

We have mostly prioritised accessibility and the learning opportunities. In Sferavis or the pipeline, we usually don’t need complex things to enter and try to match the speed. Most astronomical datasets take a lot of time to load and so we tried to make the sky interesting by adding different types of lights with scientific honesty and checked related research papers to have a clear ground of evidence. Based on real science, we have built a speedy simulated sky along with an option to see and observe directly real fits images from the survey.

Looking Beyond Sight

All we hope for is to explore infinity together through our curiosity, intelligence, and spirit of discovery. Astronomy has become incredibly diverse nowadays. When I attended my first astronomy class, my mentor introduced me to three classifications: astronomers, astrophysicists, and cosmologists. With the revolution in data science, astrophysicists are becoming increasingly prominent, while the traditional practice of observational astronomy, focused on detecting and observing the sky, seems to receive less attention. Through Sferavis, we want to inspire people to become astronomers beyond the limits of what their eyes can see.
